item.title: “Let Them” Is Not Stoicism
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

“Let Them” Is Not Stoicism

Stoic advice is never less than "be virtuous."

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Short definitions of Stoicism should not leave out virtue.
  • "Let them" oversimplifies Stoicism, which insists on fulfilling moral duties to others.

Lately, more and more people are asking for a short definition of Stoicism, and it is being summed up as “recognizing what is under our control and what is not.” What is being referenced is a portion of the ancient Stoic Epictetus’s student Arian’s notes. The Greek is ἐφ’ ἡμῖν. Or, “What is up to us.” If we expand a bit: "What lies within our agency.”

But “recognize what is up to us” was never meant to work as a summary of Stoic ethics, and it doesn’t. It offers no way to distinguish Stoicism from any other life philosophy. For example, summarizing Stoicism that way makes it hard to distinguish it from Mel Robbins’s Let Them theory, which is obviously appealing to people who recognize that their problem is trying to control situations they shouldn’t. But that is hardly all of us! (And Robbins definitely did not have Stoicism in mind when she wrote her book.)

What lies within our agency?

Stoicism’s account of agency involves, as scholars have painstakingly retrieved and beautifully explained, an account of rationality and moral development. To follow Stoicism, you have to agree with their claims about these. It is also one of the eudaimonist theories, philosophical accounts that argue that happiness is what characterizes a distinctly human life. If it were to be summed up as quick advice, it should not be “let them” but “become virtuous.” ("Be happy" would lead to too much confusion over what the right account of happiness is.)

Eudaimonist accounts do offer means to warn us against approaches to living that surely do not work. Pursue something other than virtue, like fame, power, money, and you will never be satisfied but end up hungrier for more. Something catchy might help remind us of that. But a reminder for us not to take unwarranted control is not so generally applicable. Most of us would do better to take more control of the situations around us. Stoicism is a great spur to us thinking of what we could do that we don’t. And if you think in Stoic terms of justice, our duties to others are hardly realized in even our imaginations.

The Stoic emphasis is on living up to our duties, which distinguishes it from other theories of happiness and gives it its precision. If we are going to invoke a catchy slogan, we could be reminding ourselves to make something moral of our duties.

Because if we do not recognize our duties as wives, friends, mothers, children, citizens, and neighbors, and instead look to what we can control or have power over, won't we be looking around endlessly, assessing situation after situation without virtue even in mind? We’d be scanning these situations to see when our efforts are worth it, working with no standard for what counts as worth it. And then we are not using the thing Stoicism is designed to give us.

Instead of "control only what you can" or “let them,” try “become virtuous.” Our focus then could be maintained on what counts as moral.

Imagine how helpful we could be to one another with this.

Source: Stoa/ Wikimedia Commons

item.title: How to Create Consensual Non-Monogamy Relationship Agreements
item.description:
Polyamory

How to Create Consensual Non-Monogamy Relationship Agreements

People entering CNM relationships are asking for help setting guidelines.

Posted August 19, 2026

Source: CastOfThousands / envato

Recently, I asked people on my mailing list about the challenges they had in consensual non-monogamy relationships. One clear theme emerged, as multiple people wrote in saying that they wished they had had more guidance about establishing relationship agreements early in the process of opening up.

To quote one respondent:

I really wish I had more conversations early on about what CNM meant to each of us. There is no blueprint and feelings change fast, so I just wish our agreements had been more specific in each incarnation so everyone was on the same page.

This is so beautifully put, and so true. Once you start opening up, and other relationships start to form, everything gets more complicated, more real, and more intense. It can be hard to anticipate what will emerge for you in the process — there really is no blueprint — which is partly why I advise people to treat their first set of relationship agreements as an intentional experiment to be carefully revisited with time.

Opening up shifts the status quo, which is by definition destabilizing. It’s to be expected that it will raise big feelings, necessitate difficult conversations, and highlight opportunities for growth in your relationship. One common strategy for minimizing the emotional complexity is to come up with a bunch of agreements that theoretically might make things feel more manageable. The unfortunate truth. however, is that no set of relationship agreements can protect you from hurt. Unexpected things arise, so I firmly believe the best agreements emerge from experience. A careful and intentional process will help you learn what works for your particular set of unique individuals and circumstances. Coming to durable agreements that stand the test of time is an iterative process.

To begin, center yourself. Ask yourself questions like What kind of partner do I want to be in this process? and How do I want to show up? This is an important moment to consider what your values are. What do you want to stand for? What do you want to be remembered for? How do you want to show up under stress? What do you want your before-opening-up partner to experience in this process, and why is that important to you?

Nothing should ever come between you and your values; certainly not a new experiment in opening up. Get in touch with your values; stay close to them and be intentional about living them forward. This will help you manage complex situations and provide grounding when you need to make good decisions under stress.

And remember that you can’t control what you partner(s) do, but the way you show up can influence how they respond. More importantly, if you stay generally connected to what kind of partner and person you want to be, you’ll be able to be proud of yourself, no matter what happens.

Go slow. Often when opening up there’s a sense of pressure from one or all parties, but if you want durable agreements, that takes time. You’ll have to figure out how to run experiments over time and learn from them, rather than hammering out a legislative document before taking any action. As my letter-writer noted, there is no such thing as a set blueprint for agreements or relationship structures. You’ll have to make your own and figure out what works for you. This involves time, creativity, and some delayed gratification, but it should also result in something more durable.

Create a safe environment for these discussions, as you won’t learn what’s really true for your partner if you get reactive when they tell you something. You will need to work together to create a warm and gentle environment for disclosure. Prepare yourself to do some deep self-inquiry about what’s important to you, and get curious about your partner’s fears, hopes, dreams, and desires as well. Take breaks and give one another plenty of love if the going gets tough.

Common Pitfalls in Creating CNM Agreements

  • The very language of “agreements” can be a pitfall. Instead, start thinking of this as a process of gradual and short-term experiments you run together and learn from. Craft your particular CNM situation out of what you learn works for you both. Think of this as an adventure you’re on together. Start running small experiments (very short-term agreements) and tweak as you go. You’ll learn and practice a cyclic process: talk, experiment, experience, evaluate, discuss, and revise. Ultimately, you’ll find yourself living your way into something unique that actually works for you.
  • Conflict-avoidance. A common source of problems with relationship agreements is conflict-avoidance during the agreement-making process. If you can already anticipate that an agreement is going to pose a problem for you, or you can predict it will likely be problematic for your partner, you need to keep talking, listening, and asking. Hard conversations can be scary, but they are much easier than doing repair work after breaking poorly-formed agreements.
  • New Relationship Energy (NRE). Going head over heels in a new relationship is a beautiful thing, but there’s an unfortunate tendency for people to act in self-absorbed, pushy, and inconsiderate ways to their other partner(s) while they’re swept up in the excitement. I’ve got some ideas for you about how to plan for and manage NRE here.

Come Up With a Doable Experiment and Then Another, Learning as You Go

As our question-asker accurately noted, feelings change fast. You will learn a lot about yourself and your partner as you begin to take action steps towards opening up.

  • Starting with too big a step is a big pitfall. I suggest you start from common ground; what do you both love about your relationship and want to make sure you strengthen in this process? Is there a first small step that feels 80% doable to both of you? That’s your first experiment, and once you run it, be sure to discuss what emerged for you both and what you might shift to make the next experiment work even better.
  • Don’t worry if you seem to be taking a unique path. You’re crafting something that’s just right for you, and it's too soon to tell where it will lead. Speaking from 30 years of experience in an open relationship, life is a winding path. Taking each step well is how you make sure each landmark is meaningful; it’s really not about predicting the outcome, because change is inevitable.
  • Look for the win/win. Your well-functioning open relationship will need to benefit all concerned. What experiment would help you move toward that goal?
  • Enlist a therapist or coach if you feel stuck. If you need some support with your process, a skilled helper can make a big difference. I recommend looking for someone with experience working with consensual non-monogamy.

I appreciate each courageous person who took the time to share their thoughts with me. In my next few posts, I’ll discuss other topics that came up in the responses.

item.title: The Medication Waiting Game
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

The Medication Waiting Game

Personal Perspective: The truth about finding the right psychiatric medication.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Finding the right psychiatric medication is rarely linear and requires more patience than most people expect.
  • Medications can work well for months or years before suddenly stopping, forcing you to start the process over.
  • The word "yet" reframes "nothing is working" from a conclusion into a sentence that is still in progress.
  • Persistence in finding the right medication is one of the hardest things a person can ask of themselves.

I took a new ADHD medication this morning. Within an hour, I had a pounding headache, heavy eyes, and thoughts that felt like they were running at half speed. I am currently writing this from the couch, which is where I have been all day. I’m drained in a way that not even a nap could fix (although I tried). This medication is supposed to help me focus, be more productive, and get more energy. Clearly that’s not what’s happening.

But this is not my first rodeo.

I’ve been managing meds for various mental health diagnoses since I was in high school. I've been through four anxiety disorders and years of trial and error and error and error. I’ve had more conversations with psychiatrists than I can count. So I know how this goes. The meds help, or they don’t, or they do until they don’t. You change the dose, the type of medication, and start over. And every single time, you swallow the pill with a stubborn hope that this one will work.

Anxiety Story

A few years after I was diagnosed with OCD and Panic Disorder, I started on a low dose of anti-anxiety medication. I remember being terrified of taking that medication, though, because I was convinced that my anxiety was what was driving my success. If the medication worked, I thought, I’d become someone I didn’t recognize. My anxiety, however, was so debilitating that medication was necessary. Finding what worked didn’t make me a different person. It just let me be the person I already was, just without constant interference.

The journey to getting on the right meds, though, was in no way linear.

After multiple trials of various anti-anxiety medications, my psychiatrist put me on Xanax. Within 30 minutes of taking my first pill, I became a complete zombie — physically present but mentally somewhere else entirely, like I was trying to reach my own life through a TV screen. So we tried a diluted liquid form. One drop on the tongue every morning. And that worked. Until it didn’t.

Here’s the thing no one advertises about these kinds of medications:

Sometimes things work perfectly for a year and then just stop. Your body adjusts, your brain adapts, and all of a sudden the thing that was helping you just stops working. So you have to start all over again. It’s a particular kind of exhaustion that you experience, like you are almost at the finish line and then someone moves it.

ADHD Story

I was diagnosed with ADHD more recently, which has opened up an entirely new pharmaceutical can of worms. We started by upping the dose of something else I was already taking. My executive function improved drastically, but the side effects were too painful. I was bedridden with stomach aches every morning through the afternoon. So we tried a new medication. And it had zero side effects, which was fantastic. The only problem was that I was so focused on how the meds affected my stomach that I completely forgot to ask whether they were actually working. They were not.

And then my psychiatrist left the practice. If you’ve never had to find a new psychiatrist while actively taking a medication that isn’t working, I do not recommend it. Six weeks passed before I got an appointment with someone new. My new psychiatrist tried adjusting the dose, but that led to another month of nausea and dizziness. And another month of feeling hopeless. Maybe nothing was ever going to make me feel better.

My Current Situation

Today, I started taking a stimulant. My psychiatrist told me that many patients feel an immediate cloud lifted — that they can suddenly see clearly through a fog they didn’t know existed.

So I swallowed the pill this morning with the kind of hope that only exists when you’ve been disappointed enough times that having any kind of hope feels foolish.

Fifteen minutes passed. Nothing. Thirty minutes passed. I started feeling weak. An hour in, my eyes went heavy, my thoughts became slow and thick. Two and a half hours later, I woke up from an unplanned nap, with a raging headache and the sinking feeling that this was yet another dead end.

I’m writing this four hours in, and I’m angry. Angry at my body for reacting poorly to something that is supposed to help. And angry that patience is apparently a prerequisite for treating a condition that makes being patient nearly impossible.

The Word That Keeps Me Going

On days like this (and I’ve had many of them), there’s one word that I repeat to myself.

Yet.

Nothing is working yet. I haven’t found the right medication yet.

“Yet” doesn’t make me more patient or fix anything or make the side effects go away. But it does remind me that this is not the end. It takes “nothing is working,” which feels like a conclusion, and turns it into something that is still in progress.

I am not out of options. I have a team of people dedicated to helping me figure this out. I have found medications that have worked before, which means it’s possible to find them again.

“Yet” gets me from one day to the next, even if that next day is just as demoralizing as the day before.

If you’re in the middle of your own medication journey, I want to be careful not to offer a silver lining you didn’t ask for. The process can be harder than some people make it out to be. It requires a level of persistence that seems genuinely unfair. It forces you to decide whether or not your hope is a liability or a lifeline. It involves showing up to doctor’s appointments, filling out a ridiculous number of symptom questionnaires, and explaining embarrassing side effects to a psychiatrist you just met, all while just living your life.

That’s a lot to ask of a person.

And yet…

item.title: When Biology Isn’t Black and White
item.description:
Gender

When Biology Isn’t Black and White

Science shows that sex and gender are not absolutes.

Posted August 19, 2026

The federal government now defines sex as only male or female; there is no federal recognition of gender identity, including on passports; and there are new restrictions on gender-affirming care for federal employees. And more than 600 anti-LGBTQ bills were introduced in state legislatures in the past few years, with at least 27 states enacting major restrictions or outright bans on gender-affirming care for minors.

Some say this protects children, particularly from transition surgeries. However, these surgeries are incredibly rare, and transition surgeries on genitals are not even allowed for minors in the U.S. Another concern is that transgender women competing in sports are given an unfair advantage. But transgender participation in sports is also incredibly rare. The NCAA has roughly 510,000 college athletes, and NCAA President Charlie Baker claims that he knows fewer than 10 of those athletes who are transgender—0.002 percent.

Regardless of how you feel about policy, when you ask the science community whether gender is binary, the answer is “no, not necessarily,” and any argument for gender as binary falls apart quickly when you look at biology.

Source: Katie Rainbow/Pexels

Gender and Biology

Most people like to think of gender as part of our biology. Each cell in our body has 46 chromosomes. A father’s sperm and a mother’s egg each have only half—23 each. At conception, the chromosomes of the sperm and the egg match up into 22 identical pairs, with the 23rd pair being the sex chromosome. In most cases, a person with an XX chromosome will be female, and a person with an XY chromosome will be male.

Sex is what is written in the chromosomes, or what is dictated by our biology—another word for this is genotype. Gender is what actually gets expressed—how we look, how we act, and how we feel. This is called phenotype, which is the interaction between the genes (genotype) and the environment. Sex doesn’t necessarily map perfectly to gender, and the environment plays a role in determining the gender of each person. Most of the time, a person’s sex and gender are the same, but this is not necessarily the case. And sometimes not even sex is determined by sex chromosomes.

The sex of many species is determined entirely by environmental circumstances and not by their chromosomes. For example, several species of coral reef fish like the clownfish (yup, we’re talking about Nemo) don’t have sex chromosomes at all and can actually switch genders if their schools require it. Likewise, alligators, crocodiles, turtles, and some lizards don’t have sex chromosomes; their sex is determined by nest temperature during incubation.

Physical Anatomy and Sex Chromosomes

The boys have a penis and girls have a vagina argument falls apart even more when we think about the relationship between our sex chromosomes and our external genitalia. Going back to human sex chromosomes, all fetuses start undifferentiated. At some point during prenatal development, genes on the Y chromosome cause the fetus to develop testes; these testes begin producing androgen, which is then what causes the development of the rest of the male anatomy.

However, there are cases when the fetus is not receptive to the androgen that is being produced. In these cases, the fetus will have testes, but the rest of the male genitals will not fully develop. When the baby is born, it will appear like a girl with female external genitalia, but no actual uterus or fallopian tubes. In most cases, the baby will be raised as a girl and will not know that she has an XY chromosome until puberty, when she never gets her period. This condition is called androgen insensitivity syndrome. The opposite can also occur, when a fetus with an XX chromosome produces too much androgen and develops ambiguous or partial male genitalia. This condition is called congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

This suggests that even sex characteristics are not all-or-none: the amount of androgen produced by the fetus determines whether a fetus develops male or female sex organs, when it’s produced, and how sensitive the fetus is to that androgen. There is a clear biological reason that there is more variation in both sex and gender than can be explained by a simple dichotomy of male-female, boy-girl, man-woman, or even penis-vagina.

When Not to Trust Your Gut

If scientists support the idea that gender is not necessarily binary, why don’t people believe it? One possibility is that it goes against many people’s basic intuition, or their gut. But unfortunately, intuition isn’t always right, and we shouldn’t always believe what our gut tells us. There are a ton of biases that are common in humans and very hard to shake, like the idea that coincidences are meaningful, that first impressions are most important, or that if you flip a coin five times and heads keeps coming up, tails is due to come up next (the odds are still 50/50). We also prefer explanations that are easy to understand. Explanations that favor gender as binary are simple and appeal to our own intuitions, and for many of us, to our own gender identities. We prefer black and white, and we resist the gray area in between. But in reality, most things aren’t just one thing or another; instead, they fall on a spectrum. Indeed, life is much more colorful than just black or white; it’s beautiful and complicated, just like gender.
